Richard Seewald — (1889–1976), painter and writer who belonged to Schmitt’s circle of acquaintances in Munich; see Tb 1915, pp. 524–527.
Si tacuisset, magnus Ironicus mansisset — “If you had remained silent, you would have remained a great ironist.”

Irregularität ex defectu corporis propter deformitatem — The Corpus Iuris Canonici provided for the exclusion from ordination of people with serious physical or mental disabilities (Canon 984.2). In 1983 this was restricted to mental disability (Canon 1041).
“Only where there are graves are there resurrections” — Friedrich Nietzsche, Also sprach Zarathustra. In: Nietzsche, Werke, ed. Karl Schlechta, vol. 2, 8th ed., Munich 1977, p. 369.

Walter Schubart — (1897–1941), writer and philosopher whom Ernst Jünger brought to Schmitt’s attention; see BW EJ, p. 181 and elsewhere. Schmitt is quoting from Walter Schubart, Dostojewski und Nietzsche. Symbolik ihres Lebens, Lucerne 1939. The first quotation (“Für die Wiedergeburt …”) is on p. 79; the second (“Aber in unsere Hand …”) on p. 35.

“Life draws strength from the source of evil …” — This is not a quotation from Nietzsche but from Schubart. Schubart’s actual wording is: “Life draws strength from the source of evil, but morality drains it away into death.” W. Schubart, Dostojewski und Nietzsche, cited above, p. 73.
“Song of the Sixty-Year-Old” — Beginning on 9 July 1948, Schmitt sent this poem to numerous friends and acquaintances. It was first published in 1950 in ECS, pp. 92–93.
εἰς ἄλλο γένος — From μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος, “transition into another kind or category”; Aristotle, Posterior Analytics, Book I, chapter 7, 75a38.

Herbert Guthjahr — Correctly: “Gutjahr” (1911–1944), Nazi student leader and Schmitt’s assistant at the University of Berlin from 1935 to 1939; from 1939 onward he served as a soldier. Although Gutjahr supplied information to Schmitt’s rival Reinhard Höhn, was also a member of the SS, and worked for the SS Security Service, Schmitt included him in a memorial to the dead delivered on his birthday in 1953, alongside Popitz, Jessen, Ahlmann, and others; see Schmittiana NF II, p. 291.

Prof. Trainin — Ilja Pavlovič Trajnin (1887–1957), Soviet lawyer, at Moscow University from 1921 onward, and one of the architects of Soviet criminal law. The initiative to indict representatives of German industry and business at the Nuremberg trials also came from him.
Walter Lippmann’s Atlantic “greater space” — Walter Lippmann (1889–1974), American journalist who wrote mainly on US foreign policy.

London Charter of August 1945 — The charter signed by the four principal Allied powers of the Second World War that laid down the legal basis and rules of procedure for the Nuremberg trials. Trainin was one of its signatories.
resistance through cooperation — See Schmitt’s letter of 25 August 1948 to E. R. Huber; BW Huber, pp. 339–342.

Weizsäcker trial — The Nazi-era diplomat Ernst von Weizsäcker (1882–1951) played a contradictory role during the Third Reich and later had to answer for his conduct in a highly publicized trial at Nuremberg. In 1949 he was sentenced to five years in prison.
Maquis — Apparently a reference to the maquis as a shorthand term for the French Resistance.
Henry Adams (The Education of Henry Adams) — Schmitt owned two editions, one of which—Cambridge 1927, RW 265, no. 24954—contains his annotations.
The importance of the book to Schmitt can be seen from two passages in his letters. On 26 January 1956 he wrote to Rolf Stoedter:

“Do you have The Education of Henry Adams in your library, the book from which I quoted a sentence for you in our conversation about power? I have been reading this Education since 1930, when Professor Carl Joachim Friedrich gave it to me as a gift. For me it is the finest and most important American book there is, and I knew exactly what I was doing when I quoted it at the end of my Nomos of the Earth (p. 299).” (RW 265, no. 13549.)
On 19 August 1972 he wrote to Marianne Kesting:

“For my own part, from 1933 onward I had every reason to reflect on my own situation, and this became even more intense from 1939 onward, continuing through the American camp and Nuremberg, where, as an object of American reeducation, I was reminded often enough of the well-meaning Delano. There I resolved that, in my old age, if I ever had enough time, I would write down my experiences under the title and from the perspective: Education of Henry Adams — Reeducation of Carl Schmitt.” (Publication forthcoming.)
Pareto — Vilfredo Pareto (1848–1923), Italian economist and sociologist.
“From your hands the meteor emerges …” — From R. M. Rilke, Werke, vol. II/2, Frankfurt am Main 1974, p. 132.
the famous passage about Christianity — Rilke’s letter was written not on 7 December but on 17 December 1912, from Ronda. It includes the following passage:

“[…] ever since Córdoba I have been in an almost violently anti-Christian mood. I am reading the Koran, and in places it speaks to me in a voice that I enter into with all my strength, like wind entering an organ. […] In any case, Mohammed was the closest to the source: like a river breaking through ancient rock, he forces his way through to the one God, with whom one can speak so magnificently every morning, without using the ‘Christ’ telephone into which someone is constantly shouting: Hello, who’s there?—and no one answers.”
Rainer Maria Rilke/Marie von Thurn und Taxis, Briefwechsel, vol. 1, Zurich 1951, pp. 245–246.
cum subtristes homines sunt, aut aliquantulum morosi … — “Since people are somewhat sad, or a little ill-tempered, it is time to become angry.”

quantum enses et sclopeti, arma hominum, superant arma brutorum, cornua, dentes, aculeos, tantum homo lupos, ursos, serpentes, qui ultra famem rapaces non sunt, nec nisi lacessiti saeviunt, rapacitate et sevitia superat, etiam fame futura famelicus.

“For just as swords and firearms, the weapons of human beings, surpass horns, teeth, and stings, the weapons of animals, so human beings surpass wolves, bears, and snakes in greed and cruelty. Animals do not prey beyond what their hunger requires and become savage only when provoked; human beings can be made hungry even by the thought of future hunger.”

Werner Kaegi — (1909–2005), Swiss lawyer. On 10 May 1947 he delivered his inaugural lecture at the University of Zurich under the title “Widerstandsrecht und Rechtsstaat (Zur Erneuerung des abendländischen Rechtsdenkens)” [“The Right of Resistance and the Constitutional State: Toward a Renewal of Western Legal Thought”].
Monsieur Béguin — Albert Béguin (1901–1957), Swiss literary scholar who wrote on the role of academics in the rise of National Socialism; see Albert Béguin, Faiblesse de l’Allemagne, Paris 1946.
**Today I discover § 247 in Hegel’s Philosophy of Right*** — See C. Schmitt, *Land und Meer, 6th ed., Stuttgart 2008, afterword.
birthplace of modern Bethlehem — Andrew Carnegie’s steelworks were located in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, and formed the basis of his wealth.

letter from Mr. Andrew Carnegie — Andrew Carnegie (1835–1919), American industrialist, one of the richest men of his time, philanthropist, and pacifist. Schmitt quotes from the following book: Henri Chardon, L’organisation de la République pour la paix (Publications de la Dotation Carnegie pour la Paix Internationale / Section d’Economie et d’Histoire. Histoire économique et sociale de la guerre mondiale. Série française), Paris and elsewhere, 1926.

K. Marx, Rjasanow I, p. 131 — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Karl Marx/Friedrich Engels, Historisch-kritische Gesamtausgabe. Werke, Schriften, Briefe, commissioned by the Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow and edited by D. Rjazanov, section 1, half-volume 1, Frankfurt am Main and elsewhere, 1927. A copy survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265, no. 25161.
Propos d’Alain — Émile-Auguste Chartier (1868–1951), French philosopher who, under the pseudonym Alain, created the literary form known as the Propos.

Karl Eschweiler — Catholic theologian, Schmitt’s colleague in Bonn and a friend of his; in 1933 he became an outspoken supporter of National Socialism. See Thomas Marschler, Karl Eschweiler (1886–1936). Theologische Erkenntnislehre und nationalsozialistische Ideologie (Quellen und Studien zur neueren Theologiegeschichte 9), Regensburg 2011.
Schildgenossen, vol. 13, no. 1 — Konrad Weiß, “Die politische Spannung von Inbegriff und Geschichte,” in Die Schildgenossen 13, no. 1, 1933. A copy with Schmitt’s annotations survives in his papers.
quoted in Duhourcau — François Duhourcau, La Voix intérieure de Maurice Barrès. D’après ses cahiers, Paris 1929.

Genitum, non factum — “Begotten, not made,” a quotation from the Christian Creed. Schmitt is turning against the positivists a formula that had been used at the Council of Nicaea to exclude the Arian sect.

hohoho through RoRoRo — To be understood as: homo homini homo through Rowohlt’s Rotations-Romane. Publisher Ledig-Rowohlt had picked up in America the idea of printing inexpensive books using rotary presses.

Niebel — Fritz Niebel (1913–1998), legal adviser in private industry; from 1950 managing director of the FDP parliamentary group in the German Bundestag; from 1958 onward he held various posts in the government of North Rhine-Westphalia and in the federal government.
χωριζόμενος του κυβερνήτου — “Separated from the helmsman.” From Plato’s Statesman, where the withdrawal of the divine ruler causes the cosmos to fall into disorder (273b3).
To Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 231 ff., 659 ff. “If you had been sitting with us at the table” refers to Jünger’s absence from Schmitt’s sixtieth-birthday gathering.
the little Rivarol volume you gave me in Paris seven years ago — Antoine de Rivarol, Notes, maximes et pensées (Collection des moralistes), Paris 1941. See BW EJ, p. 136.
cup bearing the inscription “To justice—always” — A pewter cup Schmitt gave to guests at his fiftieth birthday.

Qui veut faire l’ange fait la bête — “Man is neither angel nor beast, and the misfortune is that anyone who tries to act like an angel ends up acting like a beast.” Pascal, Pensées (Brunschvicg), fragment 358. Schmitt owned both Brunschvicg’s modern edition (RW 265, no. 24340) and an annotated edition from 1670 (RW 265, no. 24343).
Dahm — Georg Dahm (1904–1963), National Socialist scholar of criminal and international law.

Versari in re illicita — “To place oneself in an unlawful situation.” This Latin principle was formerly used for a doctrine in criminal law according to which anyone who committed a forbidden act could automatically be held responsible for all consequences arising from it, even in cases involving negligence.
Omnia cedunt in favorem gerentibus bellum iustum — See the note above on p. 130.

Versanti (or versato) in re illicita omnia nocent … — “Everything works against the person who is—or has been—in an unlawful situation. Everything works against the person defeated in a just war. The person defeated in a just war is in an unlawful situation; everything therefore works against him.”
Walz — Gustav Adolph Walz (1897–1948), scholar of international law. See the note below on p. 159.
In Monarchia is qui latere vult … — Correctly:
In monarchia igitur, is qui latere vult, qualiscunque sit qui regnat, extra periculum est.
“Therefore, under a monarchy, anyone who wishes to live quietly and out of sight is safe, whoever may be ruling.”
Minus saepe damnantur cives immerito … — Correctly:
Minus tamen saepe damnantur cives immerito, regnante homine, quam populo.
“Moreover, innocent citizens are less often condemned under the rule of one person than under the rule of the people.”
Ne quid ex contagione incommodi accipiant — “So that no harm may come to them through contact.” The passage refers to people regarded by the Gauls as godless or criminal and therefore avoided.
Hans Schneider — Hans Schneider (1912–2010), constitutional lawyer and student of Schmitt.

Sir Henry James Sumner Maine — Henry Sumner Maine, Ancient Law. Its Connection with the Early History of Society and Its Relation to Modern Ideas, London 1861, chapter IV. In the second edition of 1870, the quotation appears on p. 87.

poems such as “Der Nachtwandler” or “Lauschender auf blauer Au” — Theodor Däubler, Der Flammende Lavabach, in Däubler, Das Nordlicht (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, pp. 549–605; the two poems appear on pp. 583 and 584–585.
“And from attempts, miraculous flowers would spring” — Quotation from the poem “Die Verneinung,” in Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, p. 556.

beautiful definition of law in the young Hegel — “Before the law, the criminal is nothing but a criminal; but just as the law is only a fragment of human nature, so too is the criminal. If the law were a whole, an absolute, then the criminal too would be nothing but a criminal.”
G. W. F. Hegel, Der Geist des Christentums und sein Schicksal, in Hegel, Frühe Studien und Entwürfe 1787–1800, Berlin 1991, p. 509.
